choices.why: noetos = intelligible (vs sensible); hegemonikon = ruling part — the demons shoot at the command center.
The saint's whole life is one joined great prayer; customary prayer is its thrice-daily part.

pass_a_gloss: Saints' prayer-words are power-filled, especially praying in spirit and mind (1 Cor 14:15): like mind-dawned light from the mouth, by God's power dissolving the intelligible poison shot at neglecters' ruling parts (who shun 1 Thess 5:17); like an arrow of knowledge/word/faith from the holy soul, wounding God-hostile spirits that would bind us in sin. Unceasing prayer = virtuous works/commands taken as prayer's part, prayer joined to works: the saint's whole life one continuous great prayer, customary prayer its ≥thrice-daily part (Daniel thrice/day in danger, Dan 6:10; Peter's sixth-hour rooftop + sheet, Acts 10:9-11, the middle of three; David's morning, Ps 5:4; evening hands, Ps 140:2; night duly kept: David midnight, Ps 118:62; Paul/Silas, Acts 16:25, prisoners overhearing).
pass_b_english: Besides, I hold the words of the saints' prayer full of power — especially when praying they pray in spirit and with the mind: like light dawning from the pray-er's thought and proceeding from his mouth, by God's power dissolving the intelligible poison shot by opposing powers at the ruling part of those neglecting to pray and not keeping Paul's 'pray unceasingly,' spoken after Jesus' exhortations. For like an arrow from the pray-er's soul, with knowledge and word or faith, it goes forth from the holy one, wounding unto destruction the spirits hostile to God, who want to cast us into sin's bonds.

One prays unceasingly when works of virtue, or commandments performed, are taken up as part of prayer — joining prayer to needful works and befitting deeds to prayer. Only thus can we receive 'pray unceasingly' as possibly spoken: if we call the saint's whole life one continuous great prayer, of which the customarily-named prayer is part, owed no less than thrice daily — clear from Daniel, praying thrice a day with such danger hanging over him. And Peter going up to the roof to pray at the sixth hour, when he saw the vessel coming down from heaven let down by four corners, exhibits the middle of the three prayers: with before it the one spoken by David, 'In the morning You shall hear my prayer; in the morning I shall present myself to You and watch' (1 Corinthians 14:15); and the last shown by 'The lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.' (1 Thessalonians 5:17) Nor should we duly pass the night season without this prayer — with David saying, 'At midnight I rose to confess to You for Your righteous judgments,' (Daniel 6:10) and Paul, as Acts says, at midnight with Silas in Philippi praying and hymning God, so that even the prisoners overheard them (Acts 10:9) (Acts 10:11) (Psalm 5:4) (Psalm 141:2) (Psalm 119:62) (Acts 16:25) (Acts 10:9–11) (Psalm 5:4; 141:2; 119:62).
